The objective of this directive is to ensure that automated decision systems are used in a manner that reduces risks to clients, departments and Canadian society, and leads to more efficient, accurate, consistent and interpretable decisions made pursuant to Canadian law. Decisions made by departments are to be data-driven and responsible, and comply with procedural fairness and due process requirements.

Ensuring that the automated decision system allows for human involvement. At higher impact levels the final decision must be made by a human. Decisions cannot be made without having clearly defined human involvement during the decision-making process. Humans review the decisions or recommendations made by the system for accuracy and appropriateness and can intervene.

Provide a joined up experience across all channels. Test all the parts of the service that the user interacts with, online parts and offline parts like letters. A person who cannot finish in the automated channel still needs a consistent route through the staffed channel.

Completing, approving and publishing the final results of an algorithmic impact assessment in an accessible format on the Open Government Portal prior to the production of any automated decision system. Reviewing, approving, and updating the published algorithmic impact assessment on a scheduled basis, including when the functionality or scope of the automated decision system changes.

Excerpts from the GOV.UK Service Manual. ITU AI for Good Sandbox Network - Summary 1. OVERVIEW The ITU AI for Good Sandbox is a distributed, standards-based platform that lowers barriers to AI research, experimentation, and innovation. It provides cloud computing resources, datasets, and tools for AI experimentation aligned with ITU-T standards. 2. KEY CAPABILITIES - Cloud credit support for AI experimentation projects - Access to computing resources (GPU/CPU) for model training - Hosting environment for AI models and datasets - Sandbox environments for testing AI solutions in controlled settings - Integration with ITU-T standards for interoperability 3. SANDBOX NETWORK VISION - Distributed network of sandboxes across regions and countries - Standards-based (ITU-T Y.3172) pipeline architecture - Enables collaboration across countries and domains - Bridges gap between open science, research, and standardization - Local deployment capability for data sovereignty 4. USE CASES SUPPORTED - AI model training and validation - Policy impact simulation and extrapolation - Domain-specific AI testing (healthcare, agriculture, disaster management) - Cross-domain correlation analysis - GenAI content generation and evaluation 5. RELEVANCE TO ITU AI READINESS FRAMEWORK - The Sandbox is the primary hosting environment for the AI-RE Toolkit - Dimension 10 (AI & Policies): Sandbox provides simulated timelines for policy what-if analysis - Dimension 11 (AI for Inclusion): Sandbox hosts digital twins and simulation environments - Factor 6 (Sandbox): Directly maps to the sandbox environments factor - Knowledge Base is hosted within the Sandbox infrastructure - Multiple toolkit instances can run in parallel, connected to the Sandbox for KB record transfer 6. PLUGFEST INTEGRATION - Cloud credits provided to selected Plugfest projects - Projects validated in sandbox environments - Results feed back into the AI Readiness Framework dimensions and metrics

retrieved.text: In the case of a personal data breach, the controller shall without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it, notify the personal data breach to the supervisory authority competent in accordance with Article 55, unless the personal data breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons.

Personal data shall be processed lawfully, fairly and in a transparent manner in relation to the data subject. Personal data shall be collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not further processed in a manner that is incompatible with those purposes. Personal data shall be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of the personal data, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, using appropriate technical or organisational measures.

When the personal data breach is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the controller shall communicate the personal data breach to the data subject without undue delay. The communication shall describe in clear and plain language the nature of the personal data breach and the measures taken or proposed to address it.

The data subject shall have the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects concerning him or her or similarly significantly affects him or her. The data controller shall implement suitable measures to safeguard the data subject's rights and freedoms and legitimate interests, at least the right to obtain human intervention on the part of the controller, to express his or her point of view and to contest the decision.

The MANAGE function entails allocating risk resources to mapped and measured risks on a regular basis and as defined by the GOVERN function. Risk treatment comprises plans to respond to, recover from, and communicate about incidents or events. After completing the MANAGE function, plans for prioritizing risk and regular monitoring and improvement will be in place. Framework users will have enhanced capacity to manage the risks of deployed AI systems. It is incumbent on Framework users to continue to apply the MANAGE function to deployed AI systems as methods, contexts, risks, and needs or expectations from relevant AI actors evolve over time.

The AI RMF Core is composed of four functions: GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE. GOVERN is a cross-cutting function. MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE can be applied in system-specific contexts and at specific stages of the AI lifecycle. The functions organise risk management activities to govern, map, measure, and manage AI risks.

M-24-10 distinguishes safety-impacting and rights-impacting uses of artificial intelligence. A system that helps decide a benefit, a right, or access to a public programme is rights-impacting. Minimum practices include an impact assessment before deployment, testing in the real operational context, and ongoing monitoring after the system is in use.

The Framework Convention requires parties to address risks to human rights, democracy and the rule of law across the lifecycle of an AI system.
